issues.explanation: 'Object Throwing' is a weak fit as a trauma trigger for a life-threatening accident; it implies a violence/conflict cue rather than an accident-linked reminder, and it does not connect well to the rest of the profile's vehicle/safety themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now
issues.explanation: 'Outsider' is not impossible, but it sits awkwardly with the otherwise accident-focused profile and lacks a clear clinical bridge to the selected triggers, threat items, or coping responses; it reads more like an interpersonal/identity aftermath than the central formulation presented here.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is questionable for a life-threatening accident unless the patient had a clear preventable role. As selected, the rest of the profile does not support a responsibility-based narrative strongly enough to make this appraisal cohere.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: 'Startle to Touch' is more suggestive of interpersonal assault-related threat than an accident-based threat pattern, and it is not well linked to the selected accident-relevant trigger/avoidance items.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Undereating is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The active formulation emphasizes a tight Triggers ↔ Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop centered on accident-related cues and danger responses, but food restriction does not plausibly function as a strategy for the stated triggers or threats and is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: Startle to unexpected touch points more toward interpersonal assault-related threat sensitivity than the otherwise accident-focused pattern. With the listed triggers centered on vehicles, illness, and loss of autonomy, this item is not impossible but is notably weakly connected to the rest of the threat profile and trauma type.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: Guilt about not doing more to stop what happened is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening accident profile unless there is clear evidence of perceived preventability or responsibility. The rest of the appraisals emphasize helplessness and unfairness rather than responsibility, so this item pulls in a different direction and is hard to explain from the provided profile.

vignette:
Diane is a 48-year-old single woman of Canadian descent who has worked for nearly two decades as a social ministry worker in a mid-sized Midwestern city, coordinating food assistance and crisis support for vulnerable community members. She presented for psychological assessment approximately fourteen months after a serious road traffic accident in which the car she was travelling in as a passenger was struck at speed by a vehicle running a red light. The impact was violent enough to deploy the airbags, and Diane was briefly trapped by the crumpled passenger door before emergency services arrived. During those minutes of entrapment - unable to move, unable to open the door, unable to do anything but wait - she had the clear and terrifying conviction that she was going to die and that no one could prevent it. The smell of the deployed airbag, the hissing of the engine, and the sounds of other drivers shouting were all encoded in those moments of absolute helplessness.

In the weeks following the accident, Diane found that ordinary images of cars colliding - glimpsed on a television in the break room at her ministry office, or passing a fender-bender on the street - could pull her back into the passenger seat with an immediacy that felt less like memory than re-occurrence. These intrusive crash images, together with any sensation of feeling physically unwell, became powerful triggers for acute distress. Because her body had been injured in the crash, even minor physical symptoms - a headache, a racing heart, a wave of nausea - now carried a freight of danger they had never carried before. Being directed by a supervisor, asked to attend a mandatory training, or required to follow a procedural protocol at work could also ignite the same alarm, because each such moment echoed the helplessness of being trapped and unable to act for herself. These triggers, once activated, fed directly into a state of heightened vigilance: upon entering any room - the community hall where she ran weekly food distributions, the church basement where she met clients - Diane would immediately and automatically scan for exits, her eyes moving to doorways before she had consciously registered the impulse. Ordinary sounds, a door slamming in the corridor or a car backfiring outside the ministry building, could make her flinch so sharply that colleagues had begun to notice.

Diane had come to hold a set of beliefs about herself and the world that darkened everything she experienced. She was certain that what had happened to her was a profound injustice - the driver who struck them had faced only a minor traffic citation - and the absence of meaningful accountability had calcified into a conviction that the world did not operate fairly and that she had no recourse within it. More corrosively, she had come to believe that her own body was no longer a reliable instrument: it had failed to protect her once, and she could not trust its signals now. This belief that she was fundamentally helpless to prevent harm fed back into the crash imagery and the sensitivity to physical symptoms, making each bodily sensation feel like evidence of an approaching catastrophe she was powerless to stop. Her appraisals of helplessness and bodily unreliability also kept her threat system perpetually armed - if she could not trust her body and could not trust safety even when others assured her of it, then sustained vigilance felt not like a symptom but like rational self-preservation.

Out of this cluster of beliefs and sensations, Diane had constructed a life of careful avoidance. She no longer drove and refused to travel as a passenger, which in practical terms meant she had stopped attending the satellite outreach sites her role required and had quietly withdrawn from a significant portion of her professional responsibilities. She avoided any situation likely to place her body under physical stress, and - perhaps most telling - she had come to avoid relaxing, because stillness felt like lowering a guard she could not afford to lower. This avoidance, while temporarily reducing distress, had the effect of keeping her world small and her triggers close: by never habituating to the sensations of a passenger seat or the mild physical arousal of a walk to a client's home, she ensured that these remained charged. The narrowing of her life also reinforced her sense of helplessness and injustice, feeding her appraisals and sustaining the vigilance she could not relinquish. What finally brought Diane to seek help was a conversation with a client in crisis - a woman describing feeling trapped - that sent her out of the room shaking. She arrived at the intake appointment hoping, above all, to be able to do her job again, and afraid that what the accident had taken from her could not be given back.
